message.content:
In Texas, tenants have several statutory rights designed to protect them from unfair treatment and ensure safe, habitable living conditions. Below is an overview of key rights you enjoy under Texas law (specifically the Texas Property Code). Keep in mind that local ordinances may add further protections, so it’s wise to check your city or county regulations as well. | Category | Key Rights | Practical Implications | |----------|------------|------------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit, two months for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within 30 days after lease ends, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear & tear. | • Keep records of the unit’s condition at move‑in and move‑out. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, and pest control.
• Must keep the premises in a “reasonable state of repair.” | • Report problems promptly; document all communications. | | **Repair & Deduct / Rent Withholding** | • If landlord fails to fix major repairs, you may withhold rent or pay for repairs yourself and deduct the cost from rent.
• Must give written notice and allow reasonable time to fix. | • Keep receipts and send a copy to the landlord. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot enter without proper notice (usually 24 hours) except in emergencies. | • Document any unauthorized entries. | | **Anti‑Discrimination** | • Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, family status, etc. | • File complaints with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) if you suspect discrimination. | | **Lease Terms** | • Written lease required for leases longer than one year.
• Lease must include rent amount, due date, security deposit, and other essential terms. | • Review lease carefully before signing. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For non‑renewal or termination, landlord must give at least 30 days’ written notice.
• For eviction, notice period depends on reason (e.g., 30 days for nonpayment, 10 days for lease violations). | • Keep copies of all notices received. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must file a lawsuit and obtain a court order before evicting.
• Eviction without a court order is illegal. | • If you receive a notice, respond promptly and consider legal counsel. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has no statewide rent control; however, some cities may have local ordinances limiting rent increases. | • Verify local rules if you live in a city with such ordinances. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord must respect your privacy; they can’t conduct searches without consent unless there’s a valid reason (e.g., suspected illegal activity). | • Know your rights regarding entry and search. | ### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written communication, and receipts help prove your case if disputes arise. 2. **Know the Timeline** – Understand how long you have to report issues, how long the landlord has to fix them, and the notice periods for termination or eviction. 3. **Use Written Notices** – Send all notices via certified mail or email with read receipt to create a paper trail. 4. **Seek Legal Advice** – If you’re facing eviction or believe your landlord is violating your rights, consult a tenant‑rights attorney or a local legal aid organization. 5. **File Complaints** – If you suspect discrimination or unlawful eviction, file a complaint with HUD or the Texas Attorney General’s Office. --- #### Quick Reference Checklist - [ ] Have you received a written lease? - [ ] Did the landlord provide a security deposit receipt? - [ ] Are you aware of the required notice period for lease termination? - [ ] Do you have documentation of any maintenance requests? - [ ] Have you reported any habitability issues promptly? If you need more detailed guidance—such as how to draft a notice to the landlord or how to handle a specific dispute—feel free to ask!
